text: Utah News Dispatch describes Crosby as an adjunct professor at Utah State University and a project manager and consultant.
Crosby’s campaign site lists endorsements from state Rep. Rosemary Lesser, other Utah candidates, local political groups, and labor and environmental organizations.

His campaign lists affordability, accountability (including banning congressional stock trading), public-land protection, Great Salt Lake restoration, and opposition to the Stratos data-center project among its priorities.
At the October 2026 debate, Crosby criticized Moore’s support for the 2025 reconciliation law because it rolled back solar tax credits; Moore replied that he had gone to bat for Utah solar companies.
Utah News Dispatch describes Cottam as a business owner, bariatric surgeon, and consultant; The Salt Lake Tribune identifies his consulting work with medical-technology company Medtronic.
Utah News Dispatch describes Moesinger as an automation engineer and University of Utah graduate.
Moesinger’s campaign says its legislative goals are nationwide multiparty democracy and institutional changes intended to create more competition and cooperation.
In the 2026 questionnaire, Moesinger identifies ranked-choice voting and multi-member House districts as his main electoral-reform proposals.

The Salt Lake Tribune identifies Moore as the incumbent representing Utah’s current 1st District and House Republican Caucus vice chair; he previously worked as a U.S. Foreign Service officer and consultant.
Moore voted yea on July 3, 2025, on House Roll Call 190, final passage of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Moore introduced the Saline Lake Ecosystems in the Great Basin States Program Act with Rep. Jared Huffman; the House passed it in 2022 and the measure became Public Law 117-318 on December 27, 2022.
Moore voted yea on September 16, 2026, on H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act.
At the October 2026 debate, Crosby criticized Moore’s support for the 2025 reconciliation law because it rolled back solar tax credits; Moore replied that he had advocated for Utah solar companies.

Utah News Dispatch describes Bowen as an Air Force veteran who studied economics and worked as a senior IT project manager in healthcare; The Salt Lake Tribune reports he formerly served on the American Fork City Council.
Bowen identifies the Box Elder data center’s water use as a major district concern and says water-intensive projects require transparent tradeoffs.
Bowen supports an all-of-the-above energy approach and says federal subsidies should not pick energy-technology winners and losers.
In Ballotpedia's 2024 Candidate Connection survey, Cottam said a congressman's core responsibility is to pass a balanced federal budget and pledged to never vote for a deficit budget.

During the 2024 congressional debate, Cottam said the federal role in housing is very limited, linked affordability to restraining federal spending and inflation, and said communities need to allow denser housing construction.

In his 2024 Ballotpedia survey responses, Cottam said federal financial transparency and accountability needed to be restored and criticized Moore's FISA votes, arguing that government access to Americans' data should require a warrant.

In an August 2026 response to Friends of Little Cottonwood Canyon, Cottam opposed taxpayer funding for the proposed gondola, said ski resorts could build it with their own funds, and argued it would not serve the canyon's natural access needs.

A comment attributed to Daniel Cottam in UDOT's Little Cottonwood Canyon Final EIS comment volume argued the gondola would not solve summer or whole-canyon transportation needs and proposed congestion pricing plus a bus line not hindered by traffic, using natural-gas or electric buses.
Bigler retired in 2025 after 24 years teaching choir at Box Elder High School and is artistic director of the Cache Children’s Choir.
On Stratos, Bigler said she was not opposed to data centers generally but wanted more study and regulation; she gave a provisional no until environmental studies and public input were available.

Sandall's campaign identifies him as a lifelong Box Elder County resident, rancher, business owner, and former member of the Utah Farm Bureau State Board; The Salt Lake Tribune reports he has served in the Legislature since 2015 and the Senate since 2019.

Sandall sponsored 2025 SB 132, Electric Utility Amendments. The law created requirements for large-scale electric service, including Public Service Commission review of large-load contracts and protections against shifting costs to other electric customers.
Sandall voted yes on the Senate's final concurrence vote for SB 132 on March 7, 2025; the measure passed 27-0 with two absent and was signed into law on March 25.

Bigler and Quinlan criticized Sandall's sponsorship of SB 132 as helping fast-track power infrastructure for data-center projects. Sandall responded by saying he would monitor the project to ensure permits were properly vetted and would be interested in an interview if the Senate had to vote on it.

Quinlan says she studied landscape architecture at West Valley College and is a political newcomer who entered the race over concerns about the Great Salt Lake, party politics, and the cost of living.
Quinlan called for other Utah water districts to adopt conservation practices and for Utahns to conserve water to benefit the Great Salt Lake and Colorado River.

Quinlan accused Sandall, who chaired a legislative mapmaking committee, of sabotaging the effort to create fair maps. This is Quinlan's allegation, not an independently established finding; Sandall did not respond to the Tribune questionnaire.
Quinlan said MIDA had too much power and called for the authority to be dissolved; she also opposed additional data centers in the Great Salt Lake basin.

Bishop taught history and previously served in the Utah House from 1978 to 1994, including as Speaker, then represented Utah in Congress from 2003 to 2021. Republican delegates selected him to fill House District 6's vacancy in 2026.

Bishop resigned from Utah's Independent Redistricting Commission in 2021 before it recommended maps, saying the process failed to balance urban and rural interests. In 2025, he was listed among sponsors of a citizen initiative to repeal Proposition 4; his stated concern was that Utah's congressional districts should combine urban and rural voters.

When announcing his 2026 run, Bishop said housing affordability, water development and control, returning authority to the state, and reducing regulatory workload for teachers remained priorities. He did not specify a starter-home policy in that interview.
Rich leads a company providing information-technology consulting and software to businesses; Ballotpedia reports that he earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Utah in 2002.

In his Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, Rich said the Great Salt Lake could be helped through changes to water rights, improved agricultural practices, or other efforts, with state universities and the public contributing to solutions.
Rich said he wants government to make tax rules transparent and understandable so households and businesses can identify possible reductions and economic opportunities.
Ballotpedia lists the Utah Forward Party, Elevate Utah, and Trailhead to the Ballot Box as endorsements or voter-guide recommendations for Rich.

Jennie Earl is the incumbent Utah State Board of Education District 1 member, was reelected in 2022, and is serving her second term. Her official biography says she taught students with special needs and middle-school math.

USBE's December 2023 voting record lists Earl's support for a motion approving rules for Utah Fits All scholarship appeals. This is a procedural administration vote, not a vote on the program's existence or funding level.

Earl moved to amend USBE Rule R277-628 on sensitive materials and voted for the final rule in June 2024. The rule governs statewide sensitive-material removal processes; this is a historical implementation record, not a 2026 survey response.

Earl voted yes on USBE Rule R277-495, Electronic Devices in Public Schools, in August 2024. The rule requires local electronic-device policies and leaves implementation to LEAs; it did not establish a bell-to-bell ban.

At a February 2024 legislative meeting, Earl supported a substitute motion asking the Legislature to fund USBE priorities before Utah Fits All or teacher-compensation funding. This budget-priority action does not establish support for ending or maintaining the scholarship program.
The Tribune describes Callow-Heusser as a teacher, university instructor, education consultant, and former Utah State Board of Education staff member.

Asked about Utah public education's biggest challenge, Callow-Heusser named funding and said it affects class sizes, student supports, curriculum and technology, teacher support, and equitable access.

Callow-Heusser criticized Utah Fits All as diverting public revenue from public schools, raising equitable-access concerns because private schools may selectively admit students, and allowing questionable expenses; she said Utah audits had shown such expenses.

Cronin was the only board member recorded voting no on Box Elder School District's 2025 tax rate, budget, and employee salary schedules package. In remarks before the vote, she cited affordability concerns, the failed bond vote, and the need to earn taxpayer trust for future building projects.

The official April 2024 board minutes say Cronin opposed Policy 4060, High School Graduation Requirements, because she favored allowing a student with at least 24 credits to graduate from the district high school where the student completed most graduation coursework.
At the January 2026 meeting, Cronin opposed declaring Foothill Elementary surplus and advocated evaluating reuse of district buildings before disposal. The motion passed 5-1; she voted no.

At the August 2026 meeting, Cronin asked how Policy 5305 would change device use; after staff said student devices would be allowed during breaks and lunch, she moved to approve the combined policy package, which passed unanimously.

Tonioli's campaign biography says she has lived in Box Elder County for more than 20 years, earned a bachelor's degree from Utah State University, volunteered in local schools, worked as a reading and progress-monitoring paraprofessional, and taught kindergarten and second grade in Box Elder School District.
Tonioli's campaign identifies competitive teacher pay, staff support, transparent district finances, careful use of tax dollars, and lower rates if revenues allow as priorities.

On Feb. 20, 2025, as an alternate/member of the county Planning Commission, Smith said he personally favored a 1.5-acre residential-to-general-industrial rezone for a cabinet/machine shop, acknowledged it affected neighborhood harmony, and seconded the motion recommending approval; the motion passed with one dissent.
Asked about Stratos in June 2026, Smith said local leadership could not stop the project but could set clear expectations to protect nearby communities.

A Sept. 17, 2026 Weber County Hive review of filed campaign disclosures reported $20 in contributions, $13,009.67 in expenses, and a reported ending balance of $12,989.67; it said the figures did not reconcile and that the $3,520 “Gather Signatures” expense named no recipient. The report did not identify a Smith response and did not establish a legal violation.

The same review said Smith’s conflict disclosure listed multiple business entities whose state records differed in some respects, including an expired assumed-name registration and a dissolved LLC; it also noted that those differences did not establish a false disclosure. The article did not report a Smith response.
Smith defeated incumbent Boyd Bingham in the June 2026 Republican primary for Commission Seat A.

Williams is listed by Box Elder County as the unaffiliated Seat A candidate. A Sept. 2026 local investigation reported he joined a July public tour of the proposed Stratos site; it said his campaign site described growth generally as bringing both positive and detrimental change without naming Stratos.
Tueller had ten years of leadership experience on Perry City Council, according to Utah Public Radio, and said he decided to run months before public debate about Stratos began.
Tueller said county officials could have shared more information about Stratos, but that staying at the table and approving it was the right call to protect the county.
Tueller defeated incumbent Lee Perry in the June 2026 Republican primary for Commission Seat B and was unopposed in the November general election roster.
Allred reports six years as a Box Elder County deputy and six years volunteering with Search and Rescue; KSL reported he and his K-9 were injured in the August 2025 Tremonton-Garland shooting.

Allred’s campaign plan calls for weekly administrative meetings, monthly patrol and corrections briefings, individual deputy meetings, more training and equipment, clearer standards, community engagement, and possible staff changes. He also says taxpayer money should be used wisely and operations streamlined.

Allred’s campaign site says he had raised concerns and requested training and support for three years, that concerns often went unheard, and that no patrol staff meeting had occurred in six years. These are his campaign claims about the sheriff office, not independently verified findings in the cited source.
Christensen grew up in Bear River City and worked in Box Elder County with the Utah Highway Patrol for 16 years, according to KSL.

Christensen said the sheriff's office should be more involved with communities and youth and that he would work more closely with deputies and residents to identify improvements. He added that the office does a good job, there is room for improvement, and change would be gradual rather than overnight.
Shinney told KSL he had more than 26 years in law enforcement, served as a state law-enforcement colonel, and later led law enforcement at the Utah State Tax Commission.
Shinney said he saved taxpayers $10 million during ten years as Tax Commission law-enforcement director; KSL reported this as his claim.
Shinney called himself a fiscal conservative and said he would be fair and objective in resolving sheriff-office issues, adding that he would clean house if needed.
KSL reported on Oct. 8, 2026 that Hayman had told the outlet he was no longer campaigning; Box Elder County’s Oct. 28 candidate list still listed him as an unaffiliated sheriff candidate.
Box Elder County history records Young as county clerk since 2011.
As county clerk, Young certified on May 1, 2026 which county and local school-board candidates qualified for the primary ballot.

Wardle’s Utah Crime Victims Council nomination biography says he graduated from the University of Utah law school in 2012, joined the Box Elder County Attorney’s Office as a prosecutor that year, was Chief Deputy Attorney, received two Prosecutor of the Year awards in 2018, taught for the Utah Prosecution Council, and served about five years on the New Hope Crisis Center board.
Wardle said working with victims was at the top of the reasons he valued prosecution.
Box Elder County auditor history records Larsen as auditor since 2022.

Smith’s campaign priorities call for responsible budgeting, low taxes, smart long-term investments, attracting employers that fit the community, and protecting agricultural and rural character and private-property rights.

Shinney says that as MVED director he changed budget practices, bought only needed equipment, reassigned work to support staff, reclassified ten full-time officer positions to non-sworn roles, operated under budget, and increased statistics; these are campaign-site claims.
Shinney says that, if elected, he would operate within the sheriff office budget and seek ways to reduce it, and would ensure deputies are well trained.

On May 6, 2026, Young told The Salt Lake Tribune that she contacted referendum sponsors to return with a formal application; the county attorney was reviewing whether it qualified, and her office had calculated the signature threshold. This was an administrative action concerning a voter referendum application.

During a July 13, 2026 tour of the proposed Stratos site, Williams criticized the approval process, saying critics received short shrift, public feedback was lacking, and the public's will was not heard. KSL reported he joined a tour organized by project opponents; this establishes a process criticism, not a specific water-use or tax position.

In Jan. 18, 2022 Motor Vehicle Enforcement Division advisory-board minutes, Shinney described a staffing reduction from 25 investigators to 18 sworn investigators and said the division's investigation count rose from just under 3,000 to nearly 6,000. This is a historical, self-reported management record about MVED, not Box Elder Sheriff's Office.

Tremonton City Council minutes from Feb. 18, 2025 list Hayman as a sergeant with 20 years of service among the city's service awards. The minutes establish municipal service tenure but do not state any sheriff-campaign position.

Box Elder County's May 28, 2026 release says Larsen, acting as budget officer, completed the required fiscal analysis for Stratos referendum applications. The county said the analysis estimated revenue and service-cost effects and a special-election cost; these are the county's estimates, not independently verified figures.

The county's May 28, 2026 release quoted Larsen saying her duty was to prepare an unbiased, good-faith estimate and that she served as a neutral party providing factual information required by Utah law. This is her statement about that statutory analysis, not a general campaign platform.

Bloomberg Law reported that the referendum complaint alleged the impact statements issued by County Attorney Stephen Hadfield and Budget Director Larsen were biased and gave an inaccurate or incomplete view of fiscal and legal consequences. This records the plaintiffs' allegation, not a court finding about Larsen or the analysis.

A May 28, 2026 county release quoted Young saying her office began the statutory review when a referendum application was filed, including referral to the budget officer for fiscal impact and the county attorney for legal review. This documents her description of the process, not a general campaign policy on voter access or records.
